Pay is a matter of two things (well, for public school teachers).

1) Supply and demand. There are far more people graduating every year with a teaching degree than there are openings for new teachers. When the number of people with a given degree vastly exceeds the number of new jobs requiring said degree, the pay goes down because the supply of labor is higher than the demand for labor. You see this in every industry, though usually in spurts or only when it first becomes known as a "in demand) field. Networking is a great example - in the mid-90's it was promoted as an easy to enter field with high pay and lots of job opportunities. As a result, far more people got degrees in networking than there were positions for people with such a degree. As a result, the average pay plummeted. The problem is that for some reason, people aren't taking the hint and keep majoring in education (probably a combination of the lure 3-4 months of time off per year and, per my friends who are teachers, a laughably easy curriculum in college).

2) For public teachers, every dollar they earn has to be forcibly taken from the paychecks of the taxpayers. If a teacher gets a $1,000 raise, that means that the individuals paying the taxes for that school are (as a group) $1,000 worse off. Multiply this by the number of teachers in a school district, plus administrators, other staff, etc and it builds up pretty quick. There's a reason why even the people who say that teachers are underpaid don't vote for new taxes to increase their salaries, because they don't want to increase their tax burden anymore. Of course, this could be alleviated (somewhat) if we didn't have the unions fighting against teachers being paid based on their performance. Instead of a great teacher getting paid say $80k and a shitty teacher paid $40k, they'd rather have them both paid $50k (gotta take out money for the unions and obscene number of useless administrators) and give zero motivation for teachers to work any harder than they have to in order to keep their jobs.
